To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the biotinylation of the carboxyl carrier subunit of acetyl-Coa carboxylase is not a prerequisite for catalysis, that the carboxylase reaction proceeds via an intermediate carbonic-phospho anhydride and that the carboxytransferase reaction involves a conformational change of the enzyme induced by the presence of the 2-imdazolidone ring.

the biotinylation of carboxyltransfer-ase is not necessary for the catalytic function of the enzyme, and that the carboxyl carrier, biotin, is not directly involved in the carboxy-transferase-cataly- zed transcarboxylation reaction.

biotin, in its role as a prosthetic group, acts as a mobile carrier of the carboxyl group between biotin car boxylase and car boxyltransferase and that the carboxyl transfer reactions occur on separate subunits.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the elucidation of the mechanisms of the two half-reactions of the carboxylation system of E. coli acetyl CoA carboxyl-ase.
the elucidation of the mechanism of action of the acetyl CoA carboxylases.
the mechanisms of the half-reactions involved in the acetyl-Coa carboxylation reaction.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the acetyl-Coa carboxylase of Escherichi a coli is a complex enzyme composed of three distinct protein components which catalyze the following reactions: biotin carboylase (BC), carboxyl transferase (CT), and carboxyl-carrier protein (CCP) BC: CCP + ATP + HO-CO 2- ⇌ CCP-biotin - CO 2- + ADPCCP-biotin-COO- + Acetyl-Co
the carboxyl carrier biotin is covalently bound to the carboxyl transferase component of acetyl-Co-A carboxylase.
acetyl-CoA is carboxylated by a two-component system in which the carboxylation step occurs on one component (biotin) while the transfer step occurs on a second component.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

biotin, as the prosthetic group, serves as a carrier of the carboxyl group and that the enzyme-bound biotin is a substrate of biotinyl carboxylase in the carboxylic half-reaction and a substrate of carboxyltransfer-ase in the transcarboxylase half-reaction.
the biotinylation of the carboxyl carrier subunit is not a prerequisite for catalytic activity of the carboxylic components, but that biotin is required for optimal catalytic efficiency.
the biotinylation reaction is the first step in the biosynthesis of biotin and that the biotination reaction is the last step in the biosynthetic process.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the carboxyl carrier biotin is not a participant in the carboxytransferase reaction but rather a carrier of the carboxyl group from one site to another.
the acetyl-Coenzyme A carboxylation system of E. coli is an excellent model for studying the mechanism of biotin-dependent enzymes.

the carboxylase-catalyze reaction proceeds by a two-step mechanism in which the carboxyl carrier, biotin, is first activated by ATP to form an acyl-ATP intermediate and then carboxylated with carbon dioxide.
